# Hebrews Bible Study: Chapters 1-6

## Structure Overview

**I. Jesus is superior to Moses (1-6)**
**II. Do not reject God like in the past (7-11)**  
**III. Stand firm in obedience and faith (12-18)**

## Chapter 3:1-6 - Jesus Superior to Moses

### Key Study Questions
- Why are the brethren called "holy"? Are you holy?
- What is our heavenly calling?
- Why is Jesus referred to as the Apostle? What does "apostle" mean?
- Why is He referred to as a High Priest? What things did He and does He do as a Priest?
- Who appointed Him (from verse 2)?
- What comparisons and contrasts are made between Jesus and Moses?
- Why did the author compare these two figures?
- What is the conclusion?
- Explain verse 6. What does it mean that we are part of the house of Christ?
- What signs will show whether or not we are really part of His house?

### Verse by Verse Commentary

**1. Holy brethren** – God has called all believers to be holy.

1 Peter 1:15-16 states: "But as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, 'You shall be holy, for I am holy.'"

This is God's plan for us. He desires us to be 100% holy all the time. On this earth because of our old, sinful flesh we struggle for this holiness. Paul himself was in a constant tug of war between sin and righteousness (Romans 7). Holiness basically means to be separate (see Leviticus 20:26). We are called to be separate from the world and from sin. We are to be different, set apart.

Are you different? Can people notice something different or even "weird" about you? If not, that is probably because you are not different and have not separated yourself from the world's ways as you should.

Though we are in a constant struggle for holiness, it is something that we cannot achieve on this earth. Through the process of sanctification and consciously putting off and repenting of our sin, we can get nearer this target, but will never reach it until we face God and He finally wipes away all our sin. Yet the author still calls believers holy. Why?

In God's sight that is what we are. When God looks at us, He sees not our own sins, but the righteousness of Christ who swapped Himself for us. When Christ looks at us, He actually replaces our sins and clothes us with His righteousness.

**2. Partakers of a heavenly calling** – We are citizens of heaven and ambassadors of Christ. Our identity is not to be rooted in our nationality, tax bracket, or club we belong to. It is not in our favorite sports team, our gender, or our vocation. Our core identity is rooted in the fact that we are Christians, followers of Christ. We serve God's kingdom, the kingdom of heaven over and above every earthly pursuit. 

God calls us to holiness. He calls us to be a light in the world. He calls us to share the good news with everyone, everywhere. He calls us to live our lives worthily as His soldiers, His messengers, even His family members.

We are allowed to join this cause not just in the low position of an unpaid volunteer, but actually as a family member of the boss. We are children of God and are called to represent our Father to the world.

**3. Apostle** – An apostle means "sent one". Jesus was sent by the Father as He Himself attested to many times.

**4. High Priest** – A major theme of chapters 4-10 will be Jesus as our High Priest. A priest is someone who goes in between people and God, like a mediator. Jesus performed this task, bridging the gap between us and God.

**5. Jesus is superior to Moses.** Remember from chapter 1 that a major theme of Hebrews is Jesus' superiority and pre-eminence. The writer spent much of chapters 1-2 proving that Jesus is superior to the angels. Now in verses 1-6, he shows that Jesus is superior Moses.

How did the Jews view Moses? Moses was the most respected figure in all of Jewish history. It was through Moses that God freed His people from Egypt. It was through Moses that God performed many awesome wonders that became known around the world. It was through Moses that He gave the people the Ten Commandments and the entire Torah (the first 5 books of the Bible). Moses was raised up so high in Jewish culture that it was actually a problem where people were almost becoming followers of Moses instead of followers of God.

By showing that Jesus was superior to Moses, the author could show that He is indeed the Messiah and therefore worthy of praise and obedience. He gives several comparisons and contrasts between Jesus and Moses:

A. Jesus and Moses were both faithful to do all of the tasks that God gave them.

B. Jesus should receive more glory because He built the house (God's kingdom), while Moses was a servant in the house.

C. Moses was a servant in God's house, while Christ was actually God's Son. Who has a higher position, Son or servant?

**6. We are this house.** We are the body of Christ. Christ has brought us by adoption into the very household of God. Signs of being in this house include holding fast and keeping firm in our hope until the end. Some may appear for a while to be part of the house, but then fall away. True members of God's family will never fall away.

## Chapter 3:7-11 - Warning Against Hardening Hearts

### Key Study Questions
- Why does the author say that this passage (from Psalms) was authored by the Holy Spirit? What does this tell us about the authority and inspiration of Scripture?
- What does it mean to "harden your heart"?
- In what way did they provoke God?
- How were they testing God?
- What kind of "works" or miracles did they see that God did for the forty years they were in the wilderness? Did these convince them? Why or why not?
- Why could they not enter into the Promised Land (My rest)? What does this tell us about God's nature and the consequences of sin?

### Verse by Verse Commentary

**1. Just as the Holy Spirit says** – This passage is quoted from Psalms 95. Scholars are not 100% sure who authored it, but many believe David did. Yet here the writer ascribes these words to the Holy Spirit. Why? It doesn't matter who the human author is. All of Scripture is inspired by God. The Holy Spirit moved people to write down God's message. The human writer was the tool the Holy Spirit used to bring God's message to the people.

This is another reminder that all of Scripture is God's words and not mere human's own opinions. In the beginning of chapter one we noted that we cannot comprehend God on our own. Only if He reveals Himself to us, can we understand His character and plan. Because He did reveal Himself to us and has given us His message, we must PAY ATTENTION to it and take the time to diligently study it!

**2. The author first quotes from Psalms 95** about the failures of the Israelites in the Old Testament and then will go on to explain these verses making points and applications from them. Pastor John MacArthur says that he makes a 3-point exposition of this passage: firstly, "beware of unbelief" (12-19); secondly, "be afraid of falling short" (4:1-10); thirdly, "be diligent to enter" (4:11-13).

**3. The 40 years in the wilderness** teaches us about people and about God. What consequences did they face for their unbelief and disobedience?

## Chapter 3:12-19 - Beware of Unbelief

### Key Study Questions
- In what ways might an unbelieving heart manifest itself?
- How can we increase our faith in God?
- What can we do to help others not fall away?
- What specific things can you do to encourage others?
- In what ways would you like other people to encourage you?
- What does it mean that we are partakers of Christ?
- Why do you think the author talks so many times about holding fast?
- What provokes God?
- What happened to the people who provoked God?

### Verse by Verse Commentary

**1. Take care not to have an evil, unbelieving heart** – The first two words of this verse are very important. We should be mindful of every area of our Christian life. That means we should watch ourselves. We should continually evaluate ourselves. If we have any sins or sinful tendencies, we must confess them quickly before they can grow and spread. Sin is like a cancer and must be cut out mercilessly.

We learn in Hebrews 2:1 that it can be easy to drift away from God. Believers who are walking faithfully with God wouldn't typically wake up one day and then decide to commit heinous sins. It is often a gradual process.

When can unbelief start to sneak in?

A. **Not getting what we want in prayer** – We approach God with a demand in prayer. We do not receive it and grow upset that God hasn't given us what we want. Doubts may start to creep in.

B. **Facing a difficult trial** – When facing a trial, some would begin to doubt God's goodness and/or sovereignty. Any trials can cause a person to begin to grow bitter against God including the death of a loved one, loss of a job, or a painful illness. Once a bitter spirit is tolerated the next step is a complete falling away from the Lord.

C. **Not keeping a close relationship with Him** – If we are just doing the actions without renewing our mind and heart, unbelief can creep in.

**2. We have a responsibility to help other brothers and sisters not to fall away from God.** God has called us to encourage others daily. This is something we should be doing regularly as a lifestyle, not just now and then. God knows our heart's inclination toward sin. He knows the struggles we face and He knows that if we are on our own, the likelihood that we will fall into sin is much greater. In His great love and mercy, He has provided a large Christian family for us.

What are some specific things we can do to encourage others in their relationship with Christ?

A. **Phone calls** – Sometimes just seeing a person one time a week during Bible study or church is not enough. Picking up the phone is a great way to learn more about the real-life issues others are facing as well as how we can pray for and help them.

B. **Face-to-face meetings** – Invite people to your home for meals. Invite your friends out for tea or a meal. Invite other believers out to do sports or exercise together.

C. **Emails, letters or cards** – Physical cards can be a great encouragement.

D. **Text messages** – One of the simplest ways to encourage others is through a simple text message to show each other we care.

E. **During these meetings go deeper in your conversations.** Share what you have been learning in the Word. Share prayer requests. Share struggles and victories. Don't just talk about the weather and how busy you are at work.

**3. We are partakers of Christ** – Jesus said that His disciples needed to actually eat His flesh. This was an illustration for the total commitment we need and the fact that we must totally rely on Him. We cannot be His disciple unless we completely identify with Him, making Him the Lord of our life. It is not acceptable to live our life the same way we did in the past while adding in a 20-minute praise session per week. We need to imitate His character and learn from His example.

**4. Provoking God** – Sometimes we think of God as a distant being without much contact with or care about what is going on in the world. When we view God like this, we would be tempted to think that He doesn't care much about our sins. We need to realize that our sin provokes God. It is grossly offensive to Him.

**5. The consequences of sin** – Don't be fooled. God sees our sin. How does He react to it? Verse 17 shows us that it makes Him angry. This is the righteous anger which flows out of His holy nature.

Example: the people who provoked God with their sins in the wilderness wandered in it for forty years before dying without ever seeing the Promised Land. Their sin came with a high cost.

**6. Warning about God's rest** – In these verses the implication is that just as those people who provoked God could not enter into the land of rest (the Promised Land), if we follow their example in provoking God, we could not enter into His rest (heaven) either. Don't think that our fate will be different than theirs. If you have any sinful habits, know that continuing in them is just provoking God. He sees and we will also face the consequences.

# Hebrews 4:1-10 Bible Study: The Promise of Rest

## Key Structure and Themes

**Main Outline:**
I. A promise of rest remains (verse 1)
II. We must believe if we want to enter (verses 2-3)
III. This rest is a finished work God has completed (verses 4-5)
IV. This invitation is still open (verses 6-9)

**Central Questions:**
• What is the "therefore" there for?
• Does the promise still remain of entering His rest?
• What does His rest refer to?

## Verse by Verse Analysis

### The Foundation of Fear and Respect (Verse 1)

The "therefore" connects to the previous passage showing the result for rebellious people in the wilderness who did not obey God or believe in Him. They came short of God's rest and instead hardened their hearts repeatedly. God records history in the Bible so we can learn from others' mistakes and not repeat the same sins.

The first step is to fear God. As Proverbs states, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. We should respect God and fear the results of willful rebellion against Him and rejection of the gospel. However, the author is not teaching that real Christians need constant fear of losing salvation or a lifestyle of fear. Rather, we should fear IF we fall short of this rest.

**Key Cross-References for Spiritual Evaluation:**
- 1 Corinthians 10:12 – "So, if you think you are standing firm, be careful that you don't fall!"
- 2 Corinthians 13:5 – "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves."
- Philippians 2:12 – "Continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling."

### Faith as the Basis for Entry (Verses 2-3)

**Knowledge vs. Faith:** The Israelites in the wilderness had extensive knowledge. Moses taught them regularly about God, gave them the Law and divine revelations, and they witnessed miracles. They knew everything needed, but this knowledge did not profit them because it was not acted upon by faith.

For example, God promised them the Promised Land and victory. If they believed, they would have obeyed and taken possession. Instead, they disbelieved and feared the people. The lesson: **Knowledge without faith (and resulting action) is useless.**

The Hebrew readers knew much about Christ, but some remained undecided about believing. The gospel message preached to them would not help unless they chose faith in Christ.

**Application for Bible Study:** If the only accomplishment is gaining Bible knowledge, studies become pointless. Knowledge must be BELIEVED, OBEYED, and APPLIED.

**What "Rest" Means:** For the Israelites, it was physical rest in the Promised Land with peace from enemies. Since God has not promised that land to every believer (only Jews), the rest here refers to eternal life. This rest will be fully realized after this life, free from toil, temptations, persecutions, suffering, and pain. However, eternal life begins now - John 5:24 uses present tense: "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life."

### God's Finished Work (Verses 4-5)

**Completed from Foundation:** MacArthur explains, "The spiritual rest which God gives is not something incomplete or unfinished. It is a rest based upon a finished work which God purposed in eternity past, just like the rest which God took after He finished creation."

**God's Rest After Creation:** God's rest after creation was not from tiredness but demonstrated completion of His work. He established a precedent that after completed work comes rest. In Old Testament law, people worked six days and rested on the seventh, following God's model. Every seventh year was jubilee - fields lay fallow and servants were released.

**Modern Application:** Like preparing for an exam with one book left to read, or having an unfinished work project - true rest requires completion of urgent tasks. We cannot enter permanent rest with Christ until our earthly work is finished. Ephesians 2:10 states we are "created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them." God has prepared specific works for each believer to accomplish.

### The Open Invitation (Verses 6-9)

**Still Available:** Despite many people failing to enter through disobedience in the past, the opportunity remains open. The writer attributes Psalm 95 to David, who quoted it as an invitation that "today" people could still accept. The invitation remains open - there still remains a Sabbath rest for God's people.

**The Big Picture Message:**
A. Those who don't believe won't enter that rest
B. Those who believe can enter that rest  
C. Believe NOW so you don't miss it

**Biblical Urgency:** Throughout Scripture are invitations to repent and turn to God. Jesus said, "Repent for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matthew 4:17). Isaiah and Paul emphasized this urgency. The salvation message should not be delayed.

**Supporting Verses:**
- Isaiah 55:6 – "Seek the Lord while he may be found; call on him while he is near."
- 2 Corinthians 6:2 – "Now is the time of God's favor, now is the day of salvation."
- Romans 10:17 – "Faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ."
- Matthew 7:21 – "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven."

**Noah's Example:** Noah preached righteousness for over a hundred years with no listeners. When the flood came, people likely changed their hearts, but it was too late - the door was shut and opportunity was gone. The ark could have held more people, but they scoffed and wouldn't listen.

## Practical Applications

**Personal Evaluation:**
1. Make sure you have believed the message - evaluate your spiritual standing regularly
2. Share the gospel urgently with people around you
3. Don't put off sharing with family and friends - plead with them to turn to God while they have opportunity

**Discussion Questions:**
• What similarities exist between us and the Israelites in the wilderness?
• Why was knowledge not helpful for them?
• Under what condition is knowledge helpful?
• What works were finished from the foundation of the world?
• Why did God rest after creation, and how does this relate to believers' rest?
• Why could the people originally offered this "rest" not enter?
• What specific action do you need to take this week to apply these lessons?

The central message emphasizes that God's rest - eternal life - remains available through faith, not works or knowledge alone. The invitation is urgent and present, requiring immediate response while opportunity exists.

# Hebrews 4:11-16 Bible Study

This study examines a pivotal passage in Hebrews that bridges the theme of entering God's rest with the introduction of Christ as our perfect High Priest.

## Main Outline

**I. Be diligent to enter the rest (v.11)**
**II. We are accountable to follow God's Word (v.12-13)**  
**III. Christ is our perfect High Priest (v.14-16)**

## Key Themes and Applications

### Entering God's Rest (Verse 11)

The passage builds on the theme starting in Hebrews 3:7, where the good news was preached to the Israelites in the wilderness who hardened their hearts and provoked God. The same good news is preached to believers today, with even greater promises extended to us than to them.

**Application:** We must be diligent to enter into God's rest and not fall short. This requires regularly evaluating our spiritual position, holding fast to God's Word in faith, and not allowing ourselves to drift away from God. We must learn from the example of those who rebelled in the wilderness and avoid their mistakes.

### The Living Word of God (Verse 12)

Verse 12 is one of the most famous verses about God's Word: "For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart."

**Key Insights:**
- The Bible is not "just an old book" but is alive and active
- It brings life to those who obey it and transforms lives
- It penetrates people's hearts with power to change lives for eternity
- When we hear God's Word, a response is demanded - we must obey
- The Bible contains every moral principle needed for life and godliness

**Supporting Scripture:** Isaiah 55:11 states God's word "will not return to me empty, but will accomplish what I desire and achieve the purpose for which I sent it."

### God's Omniscience (Verse 13)

God sees everything we do - there is no secret we can keep from Him. He is omniscient and omnipresent. This reality should motivate obedience and reverence.

### Christ as Our High Priest (Verses 14-16)

**Jesus as Both Human and Divine:** The passage presents Jesus with His human name and divine title "Son of God," showing both His human and divine natures.

**Christ's Temptations:** Verse 15 reveals that Christ "has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin." This destroys common arguments people make when facing temptation:
- "God doesn't understand what I'm facing"
- "No one could bear up under this temptation" 
- "It's easy for God to tell us not to sin when He hasn't been tempted"

**Christ's Understanding:** Because Jesus experienced the same temptations without sinning, He can sympathize with our weaknesses. His example should motivate us to resist temptation and shows us that victory is possible.

# Hebrews 5:1-6 Bible Study

## Structure and Themes

This passage presents three main sections examining Christ's role as high priest:

I. The role of the high priest (verses 1-3)
II. The appointing of the high priest (verse 4)

The central theme connects to Hebrews' overarching message of Christ's supremacy, demonstrating that Jesus fulfills and surpasses the Old Testament priesthood.

## The Role of the High Priest (Verses 1-3)

### Key Functions and Characteristics

**1. Service "On Behalf of Men"**
The high priest's position exists entirely for others' benefit, not personal gain. As the commentary explains: "His position of leadership is used not for himself. It is not used for his own benefit, career, or finances. His job is truly 'for the people.'" This contrasts with leaders who wrongly exploit their positions, whom Jesus warned against as "wolves in sheep's clothes."

**2. Focus on "Things Pertaining to God"** 
The priesthood is fundamentally spiritual. When people sought to make Jesus an earthly king, He refused. As He told Pilate in John 18:33-36, His kingdom was not of this world. The high priest's focus remains on helping God's people grow closer to God, serving as "citizens of and ambassadors of heaven."

This creates tension for ministers who must balance spiritual and physical needs. The study notes: "Helping the physical issues should be a means to an end of helping these people spiritually." It references a Chinese proverb: "Give a man a fish and he will not be hungry for a day. Teach him how to fish and he can feed a village," adding: "Teach him about God who made the fish and he need never be hungry (spiritually) again."

**3. Offering Gifts and Sacrifices for Sins**
The high priest serves as mediator between sinful humans and holy God. He offers daily sacrifices and annually enters the Holy of Holies for atonement. As Hebrews 9:22 states: "without shedding of blood there is no remission." The gifts may refer to voluntary grain offerings showing gratitude or serve as synonymous with sacrifices.

### The High Priest's Humanity (Verse 2)

A crucial aspect is that the high priest comes from among the people, sharing their weaknesses. This enables compassionate ministry rather than harsh judgment. The study emphasizes: "His own weaknesses and sins and mistakes enabled him to treat others with mercy."

**Application for Believers:**

When tempted to judge others, believers should examine themselves first, following Jesus' teaching about removing the plank from one's own eye before addressing another's speck (Matthew 7:3-5).

**Personal Responsibility in Ministry:**
The high priest offers sacrifices "as for the people, as for himself" (verse 3). Christian leaders must maintain their own relationship with God while serving others. ### God's Sovereign Choice

The priesthood cannot be pursued as a career path. As stated: "A person could not apply for the position and seek it out. One could only be chosen for it, just like God chose Aaron as the first high priest." This divine appointment carries significant implications:

# Hebrews 1-6 Bible Study: Christ's Supremacy and Spiritual Maturity

This Bible study examines key themes in Hebrews 1-6, focusing on Christ's role as high priest and the necessity of spiritual growth and maturity among believers.

## I. Christ's Life as Our High Priest (Hebrews 5:7-10)

### Christ's Humanity and Suffering

Verses 7-10 emphasize Jesus' humanity as essential to His role as high priest. Christ suffered, cried, and prayed for deliverance from the cross, demonstrating He came not as a superhuman who couldn't feel pain or understand human emotions. Because of His humanity, He can represent us before God as one of us, having personally experienced the breadth of human emotions and suffering.

**Key Biblical Cross-References:**
- 2 Corinthians 1:3-5: God comforts us in troubles so we can comfort others
- Matthew 26:38-46: Jesus in Gethsemane preparing for suffering
- Matthew 27:46: Jesus' cry of abandonment on the cross
- 1 Peter 3:18: Christ suffered for the unrighteous to bring us to God

### Understanding Christ's "Learning" and "Perfection"

**Verse 7** likely refers to Jesus' prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane when He asked for the cup to be removed. This request was real and shows Jesus' human side that wanted to avoid the immense pain of the cross. The phrase "in the days of His flesh" implies Jesus existed before His human incarnation, reminding us of His eternal existence.

**Christ's perfection through suffering** (referencing Hebrews 2:10) does not refer to His divine character becoming morally better, nor does it mean He was sinful and became perfect. Rather, His sufferings perfected His human nature by giving Him personal understanding of what we face, enabling deeper sympathy because of His own experiences.

His earthly experiences "perfected" Him as high priest by:
- Proving He was sinless through successfully resisting every temptation
- Fulfilling all righteousness
- Setting the perfect example for us to follow
- Demonstrating things we could not have seen unless Christ became human

**Practical Application:** True belief brings obedience. Followers of Christ are required to obey Him, as faith without actions is dead.

## II. The Need to Grow in Maturity (Hebrews 5:11-14)

### The Problem of Spiritual Immaturity

The author addresses believers who had become "dull of hearing" - not sharp spiritually and having difficulty understanding biblical concepts. This dullness is not caused by outside forces but by their own choices, lethargy, and laziness. Instead of progressing spiritually, they had either stayed at the same level or regressed.

**Key Biblical Cross-References:**
- Deuteronomy 6:7: Teaching children God's commands throughout daily life
- Colossians 3:16: Teaching and admonishing one another with wisdom
- Matthew 28:20: Teaching others to obey Christ's commands
- Mark 5:19: Telling others what the Lord has done

### The Expectation of Teaching

**"By this time you ought to be teachers"** - After sufficient time exposed to biblical teaching, every believer should become a teacher in some capacity. This doesn't require the spiritual gift of teaching; it's a natural progression for all believers to pass on what they've learned.

The model follows these principles:
- Reproduction (2 Timothy 2:2): Training people to train others to train others
- Jesus' apprenticeship model: Teaching disciples who would teach others
- Every believer should be HOT: Hearing, Obeying, and Telling

**Instead of growth**, these believers needed constant reviewing and reminding of basic principles, like a piano student who never practices and doesn't remember previous lessons.

### Milk vs. Solid Food Analogy

**Spiritual babies** are normal initially, but remaining a baby forever is abnormal - like a spiritual disease. Just as physical babies are expected to grow, spiritual growth to maturity is God's expectation for all believers.

**Solid food represents:**
- Obeying known principles while digging deeper into God's Word
- Understanding more of God's character
- Applying biblical principles to every aspect of life
- Advanced applications beyond basic salvation concepts

### Training for Spiritual Discernment

**"Practice makes perfect"** - We must train ourselves to chew the meat of God's Word. Like learning to chew physical food, spiritual discernment requires practice until it becomes second nature.

**Methods for spiritual growth include:**
- Listening to sermons
- Reading Christian books
- Meditating on Scripture
- Using five Bible study methods: hear, read, study, memorize, meditate
- Challenging ourselves mentally with difficult passages

**The goal: Discerning good and evil** - This isn't merely intellectual but practical wisdom for making righteous decisions. Discernment means seeing into the heart of matters, discovering truth, and acting on that truth.

## Study Questions and Applications

### For Christ as High Priest:
- How did Christ's suffering/crying/tears help Him fulfill requirements of being high priest?
- How did Christ "learn obedience" while remaining perfect?
- How do Christ's earthly experiences perfect Him as our high priest?

### For Spiritual Maturity:
- Are you growing in Christ as much as you'd like?
- What causes you to get "stuck" at certain spiritual levels?
- How can you partake of solid food instead of milk?
- What can you do to "chew" on the meat of God's Word?
- Are you teaching others what you've learned about Christ?

## Key Takeaways

1. **Christ's humanity qualifies Him as our high priest** - His suffering and temptation enable Him to sympathize with our weaknesses while remaining sinless.

2. **Spiritual maturity is expected, not optional** - Believers should progress from receiving teaching to teaching others, following the model of reproduction and apprenticeship.

3. **Growth requires intentional practice** - Like physical development, spiritual discernment improves through consistent engagement with God's Word and application of biblical principles.

4. **The goal is practical righteousness** - Spiritual maturity enables believers to discern good and evil, making wise decisions that honor God in every aspect of life.

This study emphasizes both the theological foundation of Christ's priesthood and the practical necessity of spiritual growth, challenging believers to move beyond spiritual infancy toward mature faith that impacts others.

# Hebrews 6:1-8 Bible Study Analysis

## Passage Structure

**I. Summary of the foundational principles (1-3)**
**II. Warning against apostasy (4-8)**

## Foundational Principles and Spiritual Maturity (Verses 1-3)

The writer encourages readers to move beyond spiritual lethargy and press on for maturity. This passage connects directly to chapter 5, where the author urged believers to wake up spiritually, start obeying, and pass on what they've learned. No matter one's spiritual level—whether a new Christian or decades-long believer—there must be constant pushing toward a closer relationship with Christ. Complacency and resting on past spiritual achievements leads to stagnation.

The "elementary teaching/foundation" refers to core gospel principles, especially Old Testament concepts, that readers had been exposed to repeatedly. The writer doesn't want them perpetually stuck on the same basic points without advancing. Like a parent who repeatedly gives the same instruction when a child fails to obey, these foundational teachings had to be reviewed because the audience wasn't listening or obeying.

### Six Foundational Elements (Verses 1b-2):

**A. Repentance from dead works** - This includes empty religious rituals commonplace in New Testament times. The Pharisees had compiled thousands of rules governing every life area—Sabbath keeping, giving, vowing, and more. As Matthew 23:25-28 shows, they appeared respectable externally while seeking human honor through ostentatious fasting, prominent seating at banquets, public displays of giving, and loud street corner prayers. "Dead works" encompasses any good deeds done with ulterior motives or attempts to earn salvation through human effort.

**B. Faith toward God** - Genuine faith, as James teaches, is accompanied by works—not the "dead works" mentioned above, but natural expressions of love and appreciation for God's actions (Ephesians 2:10).

**C. Washings and laying on of hands** - This likely references Old Testament Levitical washing rules (Leviticus 16:4, 24, 26, 28) and sacrificial practices where individuals laid hands on animals to symbolically transfer sin (Leviticus 1:4, 3:8, 13, 16:21). In New Testament context, washing could represent spiritual regeneration (Titus 3:5), while laying on of hands related to prayer or receiving the Holy Spirit.

**D. Resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment** - These linked concepts were believed by Pharisees (Acts 23:8) and rooted in Old Testament teaching, particularly Daniel 12:2: "And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt."

Two interpretations exist for this passage: either the readers were believers who weren't growing spiritually, or they believed these elementary principles like most Jews but weren't yet saved because they hadn't embraced Christ. A good Pharisee would accept all these teachings without being saved due to Christ's rejection. The Hebrew audience likely included both genuine believers and fence-sitters uncommitted to Jesus.

## Warning Against Apostasy (Verses 4-8)

### The Controversial Passage (Verses 4-6)

This section generates significant theological debate, with some viewing it as evidence that salvation can be lost. However, applying the hermeneutical principle of interpreting unclear passages through clearer biblical texts rules out loss of salvation. Multiple clear biblical passages establish salvation security:

- **John 5:24**: "Very truly I tell you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and will not be judged but has crossed over from death to life."
- **1 John 5:13**: "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life."
- **John 10:28-30**: "I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish; no one will snatch them out of my hand."

Since salvation is God's gift (Ephesians 2:8-9) and not earned through human effort, it cannot be lost through lack of merit. The passage must therefore describe people who were never genuinely saved—individuals who attended church, understood the gospel, were exposed to biblical teaching, fellowshipped with believers, and shared experiences and blessings with true believers around them.

### Understanding the Terminology:

**"Enlightened"** - John 1:9 shows enlightenment doesn't equal salvation: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world." Enlightened people may understand biblical truths without following them.

**"Tasted of the heavenly gift"** - Professing believers experience tastes of Christian life. Newcomers often report feeling peaceful in church—this peace represents an overflow of what they would possess through genuine conversion.

**"Partakers of the Holy Spirit"** - The most challenging phrase to understand. Being influenced by (not sealed by) the Holy Spirit doesn't guarantee salvation. Old Testament Saul experienced the Spirit's coming and prophesied without being a true believer. In New Testament times, the Spirit works differently, coming into believers' lives and sealing the divine relationship. These individuals may have experienced Jesus' Spirit-powered ministry, the apostles' Spirit-enabled work, or the Spirit's "overflow" through church participation.

**"Fallen away"** - These professing believers eventually abandon faith, like plants on rocky soil withering under sun exposure.

### The Point of No Return

"It is impossible to renew them to repentance" presents a stark warning about an invisible line that, once crossed, prevents return to God. When these people fall away, they lack neither teaching nor knowledge—they possess everything needed for a good Christ relationship. They don't lack experiences, having experienced God's grace through church connections. Their well-informed choice becomes irreversible.

"Crucify to themselves the Son of God and put Him to open shame" may mean they conclude Christ deserved crucifixion—believing Jesus was fake like the Pharisees did, internally condoning His treatment. This extreme Christ rejection seals their eternal fate beyond restoration hope.

### The Agricultural Analogy (Verses 7-8)

This parable warns about fruitlessness, similar to Jesus' teachings about useless trees. Good ground receiving rain and producing beneficial vegetation receives God's blessing—representing people who hear and obey God's Word, trusting and following Him. Ground producing thorns and thistles becomes useless to God and faces burning—representing those who participate in church activities but bear no spiritual fruit, remaining under sin's punishment due to unrepentance.

## Cross-References for Context

**Spiritual Maturity:**
- 1 Corinthians 14:20: "Brothers and sisters, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be adults."
- Ephesians 4:13-15: Emphasizes reaching unity, knowledge of God's Son, and maturity to avoid being "tossed back and forth by the waves."

**Additional References:**
- Matthew 3:10: "The ax is already at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire."
- Hebrews 2:4: References God's testimony through signs, wonders, miracles, and Holy Spirit gifts.

## Practical Applications

This passage warns against spiritual stagnation and challenges believers to continuous growth. It emphasizes the danger of exposure to Christian truth without genuine conversion. The warning serves not to create fear in true believers but to encourage serious self-examination and commitment to spiritual progress. Believers should neither become complacent with past achievements nor ignore the reality that some who appear to walk with God may never have genuinely committed to Him.

# Hebrews 7:1-10 Bible Study

## Chapter Structure
**I. Melchizedek's background (1-3)**
**II. Melchizedek is greater than Abraham (4-10)**

## Key Biblical Cross-References

**Genesis 14:18-20** – Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High, and he blessed Abram, saying, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth. And praise be to God Most High, who delivered your enemies into your hand." Then Abram gave him a tenth of everything.

**Psalm 110:4** – The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: "You are a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek."

**Numbers 18:21-24** – "I give to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as their inheritance in return for the work they do while serving at the tent of meeting..."

## Verse by Verse Analysis

### Melchizedek as a Model of Christ's Priesthood

The author uses Melchizedek as a model of Christ's priesthood, demonstrating Jesus' superiority by comparing Christ's/Melchizedek's priesthood with that of the Levites. This comparison serves to prove that Christ's priesthood is better than the Levitical system.

### Abraham's Tithe to Melchizedek

Abraham gave one tenth of all his spoils to Melchizedek, specifically giving "of the choicest" (verse 4). This establishes one biblical basis for the 10% tithe principle. Abraham's action demonstrates several key principles:

**Giving of the Best**: Abraham gave from the choicest spoils, establishing an early precedent for giving our best to God. This principle applies in modern times through:
- Giving the best of our time to God (beginning each day with devotional time)
- Giving the first of our money rather than leftovers from our paycheck
- Giving the best of our life, not waiting until old age to serve God

### The Significance of Melchizedek's Titles

**King of Righteousness**: Melchizedek's righteous reign stood out during Abraham's dark, evil age of rampant idolatry. His kingdom functioned like a lighthouse in a storm, paralleling Jesus who came as light into a dark world. This raises mysterious questions about how Melchizedek came to believe in the Most High God and how God communicated with him, demonstrating that God's work extends beyond recorded biblical events.

**King of Peace**: This title creates a clear correlation with Christ. As John 14:27 states: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you." Jesus came to break down barriers between humanity and God, bringing peace to the world. Like Melchizedek, believers are charged as God's ambassadors to bring His message of peace.

### The Mystery of Melchizedek's Origin (Verse 3)

Two primary interpretations exist regarding Melchizedek being "without father or mother, without genealogy":

**Divine Being Interpretation**: Some argue Melchizedek had no parents and no beginning or end, making him God himself—the pre-incarnate Christ. However, the author consistently says Christ is "of the order of Melchizedek," which would be unusual terminology if Christ actually was Melchizedek.

**Unrecorded Genealogy Interpretation**: The alternative view suggests Melchizedek had normal human parents and lifespan, but these details weren't recorded in Scripture. The Peshitta translation supports this: "whose father and mother are not written in genealogies." The phrase "made like the Son of God" literally means "made to be like the Son of God," indicating his background was specifically recorded to bear resemblance to Christ.

### Perpetual Priesthood

Melchizedek "remains a priest perpetually" because God appointed him to this position, not due to lineage—similar to Samuel, who wasn't a Levite but was chosen by God as priest. This establishes a valid precedent for Christ being a priest despite not being a Levite, countering Jewish arguments that only Levites could serve as priests.

The lack of recorded death for Melchizedek signifies his priesthood's continuity, paralleling Christ's eternal priesthood. Christ's death, resurrection, and ascension didn't end His priesthood—He continues interceding and mediating at God's right hand.

## The Superiority Argument (Verses 4-10)

The author constructs a logical argument proving Melchizedek's superiority over the Levitical priesthood:

**The Logical Chain**:
1. Abraham gave a tithe to Melchizedek
2. Levites could receive tithes from other Israelites
3. Abraham represented all Israelites including Levites as their ancestor
4. Through Abraham as proxy, the Levites tithed to Melchizedek
5. The lesser tithes to the greater
6. Therefore, Melchizedek is greater than the Levites

**The Hierarchy**: Abraham/Levites < Melchizedek < Christ = Christ is supreme

This argument was crucial for the Hebrew audience who placed great importance on their traditions and Old Testament laws. By proving Melchizedek's superiority, the author demonstrates that Christ's priesthood surpasses the Levitical system.

- What is the significance that Melchizedek was king of righteousness and king of Salem?
- What does it mean that he was without father or mother? Without genealogy?
- What differences exist between Aaron's priesthood and Melchizedek's?
- Why wouldn't Moses record more information about Melchizedek in the Old Testament, considering his importance?

- What should motivate our giving?
- How does this passage show Christ's supremacy?

## Practical Applications

**Giving Principles**: The passage establishes principles for generous, sacrificial giving—giving the first and best rather than leftovers, motivated by love rather than compulsion.

**God's Sovereignty**: God can work outside established systems and isn't bound by human limitations or genealogies. He created natural laws but sometimes works beyond them.

**Christ's Eternal Priesthood**: Understanding Christ's perpetual priesthood provides assurance of His ongoing intercession and mediation for believers.

## Detailed Commentary Analysis

### The Inadequacy of the Levitical Priesthood

The author clearly teaches about the inadequacy of the Levitical priesthood to wash away sin. The Levitical system involved countless rules and sacrifices. Day after day, week after week, year after year for centuries, priests offered sacrifices in the temple. Millions of animals were slaughtered, yet this did not take away people's sin. It could only serve to cover it and offer a graphic illustration of the seriousness of sin and the need for a perfect sacrifice. Even the most faithful Old Testament figures like David could not live up to the high standard of the law. Something different was needed.

### Christ's Different Priestly Order

Jesus arose as a priest from a different order—not the order of Aaron. His coming was a clear sign that the law was lacking. If the Old Testament law and Levitical priesthood "worked," there would be no need for Jesus to come. Like the sayings "If it's not broken, don't fix it" and "Don't reinvent the wheel," if the Mosaic law could permanently restore the relationship between people and God, Jesus would not have needed to come.

Jesus came from the tribe of Judah, which never had priests. Priests came from the tribe of Levi. This was something Moses did not speak about. Jesus came from the tribe that supplied kings for the throne, as prophesied.

### Jesus' Basis for Priesthood

Jesus became priest not based on Mosaic law with its physical requirements (primarily being from the tribe of Levi). As the eternal Creator of the universe, Jesus is not bound to laws given to people. He cannot go against His character, which forms the basis for many laws, but He is not bound to the law itself.

He will not lie not because He gave this law to people, but because it goes against His character. He will not sin because He is holy. Jesus said He is Lord of the Sabbath, implying He was not under rules governing how created people live on the Sabbath. Like a parent who need not obey all rules given to children for their good, Jesus operates from His position as Creator.

Jesus is priest according to the "power of an indestructible life." He is the Son of God with no beginning or end, the Creator of the universe.

**Verse 17** confirms: "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek," verifying the Messiah as eternal priest.

### The Law's Purpose and Limitations

**Verse 18** identifies the law's weaknesses and uselessness to truly restore people to God finally and permanently. However, the law serves important purposes:

**Primary Purpose - Revealing Sin:** The main purpose, seen in Romans chapter 7, is showing people their sin clearly. The law serves as a mirror or measuring stick. By examining it, people see how far they fall short, evaluating themselves accurately by God's standard.

**Three Key Benefits:**

1. **Humbles Us:** Evaluating ourselves with the law shows how far short of God's standard we are. There's no room for pride or boasting. We see God for who He is and ourselves for who we are.

2. **Shows the Cost of Sin:** Old Testament sacrifices demonstrated that sin must be punished. This punishment was severe, ugly, and gruesome. Only God's mercy prevented personal punishment. This provided daily reminders about sin's seriousness.

3. **Shows We Need Help:** This may be the primary reason for Old Testament law. It leads people to proper hopelessness in their own ability to solve the sin problem. It leads people to God as the only source of salvation from the inescapable pit of sin we've dug.

**Key Limitation:** The law makes nothing perfect. It cannot bring anyone back to God or permanently solve the sin problem. It seemed to make the gap between people and God even larger, with infinitely holy God and sinful people having no hope to bridge the gap.

### God's Progressive Revelation

God didn't reveal everything about Himself or His plan at once, but little by little, because He is omniscient and this was the best way. If God had sent Jesus immediately after Adam and Eve sinned, while they might have accepted it, future generations would likely think pridefully they didn't need it since they didn't eat the forbidden fruit.

By waiting thousands of years, God proved conclusively that people could not solve this on their own. People had millennia of hard data and experiences highlighting repeatedly our inability to solve this problem. As preacher Dwight Moody said, you have to "preach a person into a hell before you can preach them into heaven"—showing someone he is lost and needs help before he'll accept help. God accomplished this on a grand scale throughout human history.

### Better Hope in Christ

We have a better hope through Jesus, who came as the ultimate, perfect, once-for-all sacrifice for sinners, enabling us to draw near to God. When Jesus died, the veil to the Holy of Holies was ripped from top to bottom, signifying that people now had access to God. The gap had been bridged. Through Christ, we can be children of God. He gives the Holy Spirit to indwell us. We have many spiritual blessings in Christ and should be thankful. We also benefit from history that humbles us and reminds us there was no other way and we cannot save ourselves.

### The Finality of the New Covenant

**Verse 21** shows this covenant's finality. As MacArthur notes: "The Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ is confirmed with God's oath in Psalms 110:4. God's mind will not change on the matter."

Jesus serves as guarantee of a better covenant. The study encourages identifying multiple differences between Old and New Covenants and considering how the covenant through Christ has impacted individual lives.

### Application Focus

Each study emphasizes practical application, asking what can and should be done based on what has been learned, encouraging both Bible study and obedience to Scripture for personal growth and teaching others.

### Verse 23 Analysis
Jewish tradition records that the number of Jewish high priests from Aaron to the destruction of the temple in AD 70 was 84. The total number of priests including all others besides the high priests would have been significantly higher. These would die and then another would take their place.

The commentary highlights the weariness of the old system: "For millennia there were groups of priests who spent almost their entire lives serving in the temple to make sacrifices for sins. On and on and on with no end in sight. From father to son, entire generations of priests worked continually to offer sacrifices to cover over the sins of their people. They only represented a small amount of the world's population. And they surely only offered sacrifices for a small percentage of the actual sins committed. And yet still they were kept busy without breaks or rest. That is the problem of sin and the old covenant's way of dealing with it."

### Verse 24 Analysis
Jesus is contrasted with the Levitical priesthood. The Levitical priesthood was weak and inefficient, seriously flawed in that it could make no one perfect. It continued seemingly without end but never solved the problem. However, Jesus continues forever - this represents the hope believers have.

Jesus is described as the perfect and final high priest who will never need replacement. Because He is infinite and eternal, He can perfectly and completely accomplish what thousands of priests working together could never achieve.

The commentary provides a modern analogy: "Imagine if a company like Microsoft, Baidu, or Google came out with the following press release: 'It has been discovered that our current business model is flawed. All of our tens of thousands of employees together cannot get the job done... Therefore, every single employee will be fired effective immediately. We will replace them with one lone employee who will single-handedly right the direction of the company and perfectly fulfill our vision and goals.'" This illustrates how Christ singlehandedly replaced the entire Levitical priesthood permanently.

### Salvation and Intercession
**He is able to save forever those who draw near to God** - The text emphasizes that Jesus offers salvation with a condition: He saves those who draw near to God. The word "forever" is crucial, showing that salvation is not temporary. "Once saved you can never be 'unsaved.' This is yet another biblical verse supporting the fact that believers cannot lose their salvation."

**He always lives to make intercession for them** - This reveals Jesus' current role of interceding for believers. This demonstrates His deep care and love. The commentary notes: "Satan is the accuser who accuses believers before God while Jesus is the advocate who is making appeals on our behalf before the Father."

### Character of Our High Priest
Unlike many historically corrupt high priests in Israel's history, Jesus is characterized as:
- Holy
- Innocent  
- Blameless
- Separated from sinners
- Exalted above the heavens

### His Once-for-All Sacrifice
This marks a fundamental difference from the Old Covenant. Under the Old Covenant, sacrifices were made daily with no final solution for sin. The commentary uses a medical analogy: "For some diseases there is no known cure. The patient must take medicine for his whole life... Imagine the joy that patient would feel if on a doctor's visit, the doctor informed him that a cure had been discovered."

Christ's sacrifice was "once-for-all," meaning "He already died for all of your sins – past, present, and future. He wiped them all away. He doesn't need to go the cross again." This eliminates the need for ongoing daily sacrifices and means believers are not repeatedly saved and unsaved based on new sins.

### Verse 28 Analysis
The law appointed men as high priests who were weak because all humans are weak and sinful. Jesus' priesthood is based on "the word of the oath" - God's sworn promise that Christ would be a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, representing God's unchanging purpose.

### Application
The study concludes with the practical question: "How should Jesus' character and what He has done for you change how you live every day?"

This analysis demonstrates the superiority of Christ's priesthood through its permanence, perfection, and complete efficacy in contrast to the temporary, flawed, and incomplete nature of the Levitical system.

# Hebrews 6-8: Jesus as High Priest and the New Covenant

## Structure Overview
I. Jesus' ministry as our priest and mediator (chapters 1-6)

## Chapter 8: Key Themes and Analysis

### Jesus as Our High Priest (8:1-6)

**The Main Point Made Clear**
The writer explicitly states his main point: "WE HAVE this kind of High Priest." After chapters of technical details about Melchizedek and the Levitical priesthood, the author makes the theology intensely practical and personal. This is not mere head knowledge—Jesus is our high priest. The Greek word used indicates that we actually possess Him in relationship. We are His and He is ours because He has given Himself to us and for us.

**Position of Power and Access**
Jesus sits "at the right hand of God's throne in the heavens," signifying His position of power, honor, and influence. Unlike the Levitical high priests who could only enter the Holy of Holies once per year and had limited access to God's presence, Christ has complete access to God around the clock. This gives believers special privileges and free access to God through their relationship with Christ.

**The True Tabernacle**
Jesus ministers in the "true tabernacle"—the actual place where God dwells, His throne room where His glory is most intense. The earthly tabernacle was only a copy or shadow of this heavenly sanctuary. God gave Moses the tabernacle's dimensions as a reflection of heavenly realities, with items like the lampstand, bread, and washing basin serving as symbols of spiritual truths more clearly revealed in heaven.

**Superior Ministry**
If Christ were on earth, He wouldn't qualify as a priest since He's not from the Levitical line. However, His heavenly ministry far exceeds that of earthly priests. Jesus' ministry is better than the Levitical priests because He mediates a better covenant with better promises.

### The New Covenant (8:7-13)

**Flaws in the First Covenant**
The original covenant wasn't perfect—it had fundamental weaknesses, primarily its inability to permanently remove sins. The existence of a second covenant proves the inadequacy of the first; if the original had been sufficient, God wouldn't have established another.

**Israel's Disobedience**
The Jews consistently failed to obey the first covenant. Throughout most of the Old Testament period, they continued in disobedience, ultimately rejecting Jesus when He came. Currently, only around 2% of Israel's population believes in Jesus as Messiah, demonstrating widespread rejection of Christ.

**Characteristics of the New Covenant**
The New Covenant is fundamentally internal rather than external. Key distinguishing marks include:

1. **Internal transformation**: God will put His laws in their minds and write them on their hearts
2. **Personal relationship**: "I will be their God, and they will be my people"
3. **Universal knowledge**: "No longer will they teach their neighbor, or say to one another, 'Know the Lord,' because they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest"
4. **Complete forgiveness**: "I will forgive their wickedness and will remember their sins no more"

**Future Fulfillment**
Although Israel currently rejects Jesus, this is temporary. God promises throughout Scripture to restore Israel to Himself. Just prior to Christ's second coming, tribulations and judgments will affect a large percentage of Israel's population, and the remnant will accept Jesus. At the beginning of Jesus' millennial reign, all remaining Jews will believe in Christ.

**Present Application**
The New Covenant's internal nature serves as a reminder that Christian faith isn't about external religious activities—attending church, public prayer, or traditions that appear religious to others. True faith involves maintaining a close heart relationship with God. As God told Samuel, "Man looks at the outside, but God looks at the heart."

The internal nature of the New Covenant calls for heart examination—ensuring faith is genuine rather than merely external religious observance.

# Hebrews 9:1-14 Bible Study

## Passage Structure
**I. Description of the earthly tabernacle (1-5)**
**II. Weaknesses of the earthly tabernacle/system (6-10)**
**III. Our eternal redemption through Christ who entered the Holy of Holies on our behalf (11-14)**

## The Earthly Tabernacle and Worship (Verses 1-5)

### Purpose and Function
One of the key purposes of the tabernacle was to be a reminder to people about the need to worship God. Many of the objects inside were related to worship. God created us to worship Him from the beginning. In Revelation 7:9-12 we can see that God's "end vision" for the world is to make worshipers of Himself of every tribe and tongue.

### Daily Worship Application
Many times, we stress the eternal importance of sharing the gospel or building the church. Yet sometimes we forget that the even more basic daily duty we have of worshiping and praising God. This is not a "once-a-week" activity we do during church. The Psalms are full of instances of David and the other writers worshiping God privately. Worship can be public. But our worship in public will likely not be real or heartfelt unless we also worship God in our homes during our own personal time with the Lord.

### Tabernacle Components and Significance
The earthly tabernacle was a shadow of the heavenly one. Many of the objects inside have deep spiritual significance:
- **Bread of Life**: "Then Jesus declared, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never go hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.'" (John 6:35)
- **Light of the World**: "When Jesus spoke again to the people, he said, 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.'" (John 8:12)
- **Incense and Prayer**: "The smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of God's people, went up before God from the angel's hand." (Revelation 8:4)

## Limitations of the Old System (Verses 6-10)

### Priestly Service and Restrictions
The priests serve continually in the holy place. Part of their tasks include replacing the bread daily, lighting the lamps, and keeping the incense going. It is a continuous service before the Lord. Yet they could only enter into the Holy of Holies once per year. Then only the high priest could enter. This was the day of atonement. The priest would take blood to sprinkle onto the ark of the covenant. This was offered to cover all of the sins which had been committed unknowingly by the Israelite congregation in the past year.

### Limited Access to God
The Levitical system did not provide any direct access into God's presence for His people. Rather, it kept them away. The Holy Spirit taught concerning the tabernacle that it teaches how inaccessible God is apart from the death of Jesus Christ. By the Spirit-inspired instruction given for the Holiest of All, He was indicating that there was no way to God in the ceremonial system. Only Christ could open the way (John 14:6). The priests were limited in their access to God. Only one could go once per year. Now through Christ we can all come to God directly at any time.

### Inadequate Conscience Cleansing
The gifts and sacrifices offered in the tabernacle could not truly make people perfect in conscience. Their sins were covered, but not really taken away or replaced. These sacrifices could not take away a guilty conscience. The sacrifices merely foreshadowed what would one day be the true sacrifice: Christ.

Why couldn't the sacrifices take away a guilty conscience? They couldn't because they were external, not internal. People's hearts needed to be changed. No amount of sacrifices, washings, food, or rules for cleanliness could change a person's heart. This is clearly seen in the case of the Pharisees, who did all of these rituals, but whose hearts were like a tomb (Matthew 23:13-27).

## Christ's Perfect Sacrifice (Verses 11-14)

### The Turning Point
"But" - Here is that all-important word. Just when things looked the bleakest, Christ appeared. He didn't appear with a lot of fanfare. He just came and what He did changed the world.

### Christ as High Priest
He is the high priest of good things to come. In James 1:17 we learn that every good gift is from above. Jesus is the priest who mediates between us and God and bestows upon us the good gifts of God.

### Superior Tabernacle
Jesus entered a "greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say not of this creation." The focus is on the comparison between what Jesus did (offer atonement for us with His own blood) versus what the Levites did. Instead of offering the blood of animals, He offered His own.

### Key Characteristics of Christ's Sacrifice

**Through His Own Blood**: He sacrificed Himself in the most excruciatingly painful way imaginable.

**Once for All**: Jesus doesn't need to go into the holy place on a yearly basis. Once was enough. Jesus' blood sacrifice was so intensely effective that His blood is enough for all time. "For the life of a creature is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for yourselves on the altar; it is the blood that makes atonement for one's life." (Leviticus 17:11)

**Voluntary Offering**: Jesus offered Himself - It wasn't His responsibility. He didn't have to. He chose to because of His love for us.

**Without Blemish**: Jesus was the perfect Lamb of God, innocent and unstained by the world.

### Conscience Cleansing
Christ's sacrifice cleanses our conscience. Key biblical insights on conscience:
- "The human spirit is the lamp of the Lord that sheds light on one's inmost being." (Proverbs 20:27)
- "They show that the requirements of the law are written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness" (Romans 2:15)

Conscience can be shaped by our environment, so it's crucial to tune it correctly according to God's Word. Parents should shape their children's consciences. The purpose of having a clean conscience is to serve the living God effectively.

**Hebrews 11:1-7 Bible Study: We Must Have Faith to Please God**

**Chapter Context and Structure**
This chapter connects directly to chapter 10 and leads into chapter 12:1, forming a crucial bridge in the book's argument about faith's essential role in the Christian life. Hebrews 11 serves as the definitive biblical exposition on faith in action through the examples of Old Testament patriarchs.

**Definition and Nature of Faith**
Faith is defined as "assurance" of things hoped for and "conviction" of things not seen. This biblical faith is neither irrational nor blind. God provides evidence of His existence through creation (Psalm 19) and other means. Jesus often provided evidence for belief, most notably "the Sign of Jonah." When Gideon asked for signs, God graciously provided multiple confirmations.

Faith is reasonable and logical, though not 100% provable. While there are substantial evidences and reasons to believe in God's existence, some element of faith remains necessary. Faith involves being convinced of something unseen, supported by evidence but requiring trust beyond complete proof.

Verse 2 demonstrates this principle: "by faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible."

**Old Testament Examples of Faith**

**Abel (Genesis 4:1-15)**
Abel's sacrifice was superior to Cain's because God accepted it while rejecting Cain's offering. Though the Bible doesn't explicitly detail God's instructions about sacrifices, it's reasonable to assume God had communicated His expectations. Cain's offering represented the first instance of man-made religion, similar to Aaron's sons who offered "strange fire" before the Lord (Leviticus 10:1). Abel's faith demonstrated proper worship according to God's standards.

**Enoch (Genesis 5:18-24)**
The text describes Enoch as one who "walked with God" during the pre-flood era when "the thoughts of people's hearts were evil continually." This was arguably a more wicked generation than today, far removed from the Garden of Eden. Stories from Adam were becoming distant memories, and direct divine interaction was rare.

While most people mocked and scorned the unseen God, Enoch remained faithful. He "followed the light when most people sought to extinguish it." As a result, God took him directly to heaven without experiencing death.

**Universal Nature of Faith**
Everyone exercises faith daily; the crucial question is where that faith is placed. Scientists who teach evolution make numerous unsubstantiated assumptions: that something (the Big Bang) came from nothing, that life began randomly without explanation of when, where, or how, and that energy arose from non-energy independently.

Daily life requires constant faith: trusting airline pilots never met, riding with Uber drivers on busy roads, sitting on chairs expecting them to hold weight, or assuming salary deposits appear without verification. Those who deny faith's necessity deceive themselves.

**Faith in Action vs. Lack of Faith**
Hebrews 11 presents numerous examples of believers exercising extraordinary faith in challenging circumstances. Similar examples exist today among modern believers who demonstrate remarkable trust in God through their actions.

Conversely, certain behaviors reveal lack of faith: compromising moral standards to preserve employment instead of trusting God's provision, excessive worry about the future, or relying solely on human understanding without prayer.

# Hebrews 12:1-11 Bible Study: Running the Race with Endurance and God's Discipline

## I. Run the Race with Endurance (12:1-3)

### The Great Cloud of Witnesses

The "therefore" in verse 1 directly connects to Hebrews 11, where the author presented examples of faithful Old Testament saints. These believers form a "so great a cloud of witnesses" - not necessarily actively watching us from heaven, but providing powerful examples that their lives demonstrated it was possible to face trials and adversities in this world and conquer them by faith. They were not "super-believers" who never sinned, but faithful believers who chose to have faith in God even when it wasn't easy.

**Illustration**: Imagine a rookie baseball player at Boston's Fenway Park, getting ready for his first game. His coach reminds him of all the baseball greats who have stood in that same spot beside home plate. This inspires the rookie to do his absolute best to follow in the footsteps of baseball heroes. Similarly, the writer motivates believers by showing it is possible to live faithful lives even in the midst of a crooked and dark generation.

### Laying Aside Every Encumbrance

An encumbrance is not necessarily a sin - it's something that slows an athlete down in a race. 

**Illustration**: A marathon runner arrives at the starting line with a large backpack containing a CD player, portable fan, extra clothes, and other "good" things. Are these bad? Not necessarily, but they are unnecessary and slow him down.

The Christian life requires evaluating what activities we may need to cut out to be most productive. We should be willing to say "no" to things that may encumber us, even when they aren't sinful. Do not allow "good" things to keep you from the best thing.

### The Sin Which Easily Entangles

Sin is sneaky and easy to begin tolerating. It builds a wall between us and God, keeping us from being effective in service. We must be quick to recognize sin and repent of it.

### Running with Endurance

The Christian life is not a sprint, but a marathon. Each saint in Hebrews 11 faced many challenges, trials, and temptations. Sometimes they stumbled, but they got back up and finished the race. Unfortunately, many professing believers fall away. Statistics show that most Christian workers (pastors or missionaries) leave the ministry at some point, reminding us how difficult it is to persevere.

### Fixing Our Eyes on Jesus

The solution to developing endurance is found in fixing our eyes on Jesus. We must not be like Peter who took his eyes off Jesus when walking on water, saw the crashing waves, and began to sink when his faith faltered. The same will happen if we focus on circumstances and the world around us instead of on Jesus.

Jesus is our perfect example of endurance. Throughout His ministry He was doubted, scoffed at, mocked, challenged, and persecuted. Finally, He faced the most shameful, humiliating, and painful death imaginable. He endured all this "for the joy set before Him" - likely referring to His bride, the church. Jesus' death redeemed us to Himself. Our salvation was worthy enough that Jesus would face every indignation and suffering to accomplish our salvation.

**Application**: We should consider and meditate on Jesus' example. This should prevent us from growing weary or losing heart. We should persevere in whatever God is calling us to do.

## II. God Disciplines His Sons (12:4-11)

### The Context of Discipline

Verse 4 reminds readers that none of them had yet given their lives (been martyred) for their faith. They had not paid the ultimate price or been tested with the ultimate test yet. If the saints in Hebrews 11 could endure to the end, some to the point of martyrdom, so should they.

### The Motivation Behind Discipline

Some readers had forgotten about God's discipline, perhaps surprised to face consequences of sin. Maybe they had been taught that belief in God guaranteed health, wealth, and happiness. The author first establishes that the motivation of discipline is love. Teaching about God's discipline is not incompatible with teaching about God's love - it shows another aspect and the depth of His love.

The most important exhortation is: "do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord." We shouldn't cast it aside or be surprised when we face it. Instead of fainting ("I can't bear it!"), we should take it as a reminder that we are His children and correct the issue that needs addressing.

### The Nature of Discipline

The trials these believers faced may have been discipline from God. Discipline has two meanings:
1. Punishment for correction against one who has sinned
2. Training (like being disciplined to wake up at 5:00am daily for exercise)

These sufferings may have been direct results of sin, or they may fall into the general category of trials God uses to train believers to endure and strengthen their faith.

### Universal Discipline

"What son is there whom his father does not discipline?" implies that all parents SHOULD discipline their children. While the main thrust isn't teaching parents to discipline children, this is a secondary application. If parents love their children, they must discipline them. It is loving TO discipline because love is willing to do what is necessary for others' good, no matter how difficult or inconvenient.

Verse 8 indicates that if we are never disciplined by God, we don't belong to Him.

### Results of Proper Discipline

Verse 9 implies that children will respect parents who faithfully discipline them. Contrary to worldly thinking, discipline doesn't hurt the parent-child relationship or create resentment. Children have security when they know boundaries that are consistently enforced. They see their parents' love through faithful discipline.

We must subject ourselves to God, accepting correction and submitting to His authority from our hearts. This shows clearly one aspect of our relationship with God - He is not merely a friend or powerful Santa Claus, but our authority to whom we must submit.

### The Purpose of Discipline

Verses 10-11 reveal discipline's purpose. God's discipline is not punitive, shameful, hurtful, vengeful, or an outlet for anger. The goal is correction and holiness.

For parents, this means discipline must be combined with clear teaching aimed at the heart, not just external behavior. For believers, this is comforting - God doesn't discipline because He enjoys it, but always for our good so we become more holy.

Verse 11 acknowledges that experiencing or giving discipline is not pleasant, but it bears fruit. It accomplishes its purpose by changing hearts and lives. Notice "trained" indicates a continuous process, not a one-time event.

## Cross-References on Endurance

**Colossians 1:11**: "Being strengthened with all power according to his glorious might so that you may have great endurance and patience."

**James 5:11**: "As you know, we count as blessed those who have persevered. You have heard of Job's perseverance and have seen what the Lord finally brought about. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy."

**Proverbs 6:23**: "For this command is a lamp, this teaching is a light, and correction and instruction are the way to life."

**2 Timothy 3:12**: "In fact, everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted."

**Philippians 1:29**: "For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him."

## Applications

1. **For Running the Race**: Evaluate what "good" things might be encumbrances in your spiritual race. Practice fixing your eyes on Jesus daily through prayer, Scripture reading, and meditation on His example.

2. **For Discipline**: When facing trials, consider whether God might be disciplining you for correction or training. Submit to His authority and seek to learn from the experience.

3. **For Parents**: Discipline children out of love, combining correction with clear teaching, aiming for heart change rather than mere behavioral compliance.

4. **For Endurance**: Remember that the Christian life is a marathon requiring perseverance. Draw strength from the examples of faithful believers who have gone before us.
